“I, however, believe that the Jewish people, both because of the location of their land … and because of their religion … had a greater right to rule over the gentiles than the Romans did.”
Guido Vernani da Rimini, Il più antico oppositore politico di Dante. Testo critico del “De Reprobatione Monarchiae”, ed. Nevio Matteini, Padua 1958, p. 106.
“Desecration of my name” — See below, note to p. 309.

Tiso — Jozef Tiso (1887–1947), Catholic priest and, from 1939 to 1945, president of the First Slovak Republic, which collaborated with Hitler. After the war he was sentenced to death by a people’s court as a war criminal and executed. Schmitt’s claim that the Pope showed no interest in his case is false; an appeal for clemency by Pius XII was rejected.
Julius Rosenberg — (1918–1953), executed in the United States as a Soviet spy. Pope Pius XII unsuccessfully appealed on his behalf.

“Black-market work is my delight! …” — A parody of the fourth stanza of Eichendorff’s poem “Heimweh.” See Joseph von Eichendorff, Gedichte Versepen, ed. Hartwig Schultz, Frankfurt am Main 1987, p. 253:
Morning is my delight! In the quiet hour I climb to the highest mountain and look into the distance, and from my heart I greet you, Germany!
Error in persona — “mistake about the identity of the person”; a term used in criminal law.
“Heraclitus says this” — Fragment 54. In: Hermann Diels, ed., Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, Berlin 1903, p. 74.

Le secret de l’église catholique … — An allusion to Villiers de l’Isle-Adam; see above, note to p. 251. Schmitt wrote the sentence in Armin Mohler’s guest book in Paris on 9 May 1960; see BW d’Ors, p. 146.

Bodin: de ne jamais braver la fureur populaire — “never to defy popular fury.” Schmitt quotes from Jean Bodin, Oeuvres philosophiques, text established, translated, and published by Pierre Mesnard, Corpus général des philosophes français: Auteurs modernes, 5/3, Paris 1951; annotated copy in the Schmitt papers, RW 265 no. 26970.

Galeazzi-Lisi — Dr. Roberto Galeazzi-Lisi (1891–1968), personal physician to Pius XII. Among other treatments, he used the fresh-cell therapy developed by Paul Niehans and supplied tabloid newspapers with reports about the Pope’s final agony.

“in the form of a Jewish remigrant” — The reference is to Karl Löwenstein (1891–1973), who in 1945, as a legal adviser to the American military government, pushed for Schmitt’s arrest and the confiscation of his library. See Martin Tielke, “Die Bibliothek Carl Schmitts.” In: Schmittiana NF I, 2011, pp. 294 ff.

Simone Weil — (1909–1943), French philosopher and mystic. Born Jewish, she moved toward Catholicism without formally converting. Schmitt is probably referring to her book Das Unglück und die Gottesliebe, translated by Friedhelm Kemp, Munich 1953; copy in the Schmitt papers, RW 265 no. 23477. See also Karl Epting, Der geistliche Weg der Simone Weil, Stuttgart 1955; copy in the Schmitt papers, RW 265 no. 23454.

Epting — Karl Epting (1905–1979), scholar of Romance languages, active in National Socialist cultural policy in occupied France and head of the German Institute in Paris from 1940 to 1945. From 1946 to 1949 he was imprisoned in the French military prison Cherche-Midi. From 1949 to 1951 he worked as an editor at Greven-Verlag in Cologne, where he was responsible for Carl Schmitt’s works.

“Gueydan’s essay” — William [Guillermo] Gueydan de Roussel, “Leviathan et Homo. Hommage à Carl Schmitt.” In: Epirrhosis. Festschrift zum 65. Geburtstag am 11. 7. 1953, unpublished and inconsistently paginated typescript; Schmitt papers, RW 265 no. 21368.

Quare existimamus nos sensus (a quo omnia in naturalibus petenda sunt, nisi forte libeat insanire) antistites religiosos, et oraculorum ejus non imperitos interpretes, nos praestitisse: ut alii professione quadam, nos re ipsa, sensum tueri ac colere videamur.

“For this reason I consider myself, as it were, a faithful priest of the senses — from which all knowledge of natural things must be drawn unless one wishes to go mad — and no unskilled interpreter of their oracles.”
Francis Bacon, Neues Organon, Latin-German ed. Wolfgang Krohn, Hamburg 1990, part 1, pp. 48–49.
Deinde etiam, tu scelere haud minore stultitiae apotheosin introduxisti, et vilissimas cogitationes religione munire ausus es.
“Then, in an offense no less serious, you introduced the deification of stupidity and dared to protect the vilest thoughts with religion.”
Francis Bacon, The Works of Francis Bacon, collected and edited by J. Spedding, R. L. Ellis, and D. D. Heath, vol. 3, London 1870, p. 531.
Parte alia, amissis Troilus armis, Infelix puer atque impar congressus Achilli.
Virgil, Aeneid, Book 1, lines 474–75. In Voss’s translation:
“There too is Troilus, fleeing after losing his armor, an unhappy boy, unequal when he met Achilles.”
Nec tibi quam bellum longior ira fuit — From a distich by Marco Antonio Casanova on Pope Julius II:
Una dedit bellum, bellum lux sustulit una, Nec tibi quam bellum longior ira fuit.
“One day gave the war, one day brought the war to an end, and your anger lasted no longer than the war.”
Quoted in Joseph de Maistre, Du Pape, 9th ed., Lyon and Paris 1853, p. 192.
Pompeio scelus est bellum civile perempto / Quo fuerat vivente fides —
“After Pompey’s death, civil war is a crime; while he lived, it had been a proof of our loyalty.”

“see Mirbt” — Schmitt is referring to Carl Mirbt, Quellen zur Geschichte des Papsttums und des römischen Katholizismus, 3rd rev. and expanded ed., Tübingen 1911; annotated copy in the Schmitt papers, RW 265 no. 26089.

“Essay by Jürgen Habermas” — J. Habermas, “Mit Heidegger gegen Heidegger denken.” In: Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, 25 July 1953. In this review of Heidegger’s Einführung in die Metaphysik, Habermas protested against the unannotated republication of a Heidegger text dating from the 1930s. See BW Forsthoff, p. 97; van Laak, p. 89.
“Two souls and one thought …” — Inspired by Friedrich Halm, Gedichte, Stuttgart and Tübingen 1850, p. 165:
My heart, I want to ask you: what is love? Tell me true. “Two souls and a single thought, two hearts that beat as two.”
Moju — Moritz Julius Bonn; see 26 December 1953. The words “has meanwhile triumphed” probably refer to the publication of M. J. Bonn, So macht man Geschichte, Munich 1953.

“Attack in Das Schwarze Korps” — The SS sharply attacked Schmitt twice in its journal at the end of 1936: “Eine peinliche Ehrenrettung,” Das Schwarze Korps, 3 December 1936; and “Es wird immer noch peinlicher,” ibid., 10 December 1936.
Vestrum scelus, meus somnus — Augustine, De civitate Dei, Book 17, chapter 18:
Quid agitis vani? Quod vestrum scelus erit, meus somnus erit.
“What are you doing, vain men? What is your crime will be only my sleep.”
Aurelius Augustine, Vom Gottesstaat, trans. Wilhelm Thimme, Munich 1978, vol. 2, p. 405.
“Ps. 40:6” — This follows the numbering of the Vulgate. In modern numbering: Psalm 41:6.
“Being and appearance …” — After Ferdinand Hardekopf, “Zwiegespräch.” In: idem, Gesammelte Dichtungen, Zurich 1963, p. 169:

Dialogue became a magic text, a necromancer’s play; from both sides there was conjured forth whatever pleased the spirit, whatever seemed an appearance to the senses, whatever appearance itself devised. Appearance gave meaning, and meaning gave it appearance, and time passed away.
δόξα — “opinion,” in the sense of mere opinion, illusion, or appearance.
“I am reading Ch. Fourier” — Charles Fourier, Théorie de l’unité universelle, Oeuvres complètes, vol. 4, Paris 1841, pp. 407 ff.
Loin de ce calme plat … — Ibid., p. 399.

“this McCarthy” — Joseph McCarthy (1908–1957), Republican senator from Wisconsin whose name became associated with the anti-communist campaign in the United States in the early 1950s. Schmitt also described the episode on the train in a letter to Walter Petwaidic dated 10 September 1953, printed in Kai Burkhardt, ed., Carl Schmitt und die Öffentlichkeit. Briefwechsel mit Journalisten, Publizisten und Verlegern aus den Jahren 1923 bis 1983, Berlin 2013, p. 121.
“Only he who can conquer …” — See above, note to p. 236.
“re-education of Carl Schmitt” — See above, note to p. 136.
“In Theodor Wiesengrund Adorno’s Minima Moralia” — Th. W. Adorno, Minima Moralia, Frankfurt am Main 1969, p. 255.
Petwaidic — Walter Petwaidic (1904–1978), who wrote under the pseudonym Walter Fredericia, journalist at the weekly newspaper Die Zeit.
Bourdin — Paul Bourdin (1900–1955), editor-in-chief of Die Welt and commentator for the weekly newspaper Die Zeit.

“Statement by Lorenz von Stein” — Schmitt refers to Lorenz von Stein, Geschichte der sozialen Bewegung in Frankreich von 1789 bis auf unsere Tage, ed. Gottfried Salomon, Munich 1921, vol. 2, p. 11; annotated copy in the Schmitt papers, RW 265 no. 25087. See C. Schmitt, “Die Stellung Lorenz von Steins in der Geschichte des 19. Jahrhunderts.” In: SGN, pp. 156–65.
“Federal Constitutional Court judgment of 17 December 1953” — The judgment held that all civil-service employment relationships had ended on 8 May 1945.

Le Pal — Title of a weekly newspaper written entirely by Léon Bloy, of which four issues appeared in 1885. A fifth issue was assembled in 1935 from texts Bloy had intended for it. A new annotated complete edition appeared in 1979: L. Bloy, Le Pal, notes and prefaces by Daniel Habrekorn, complete edition revised and corrected against the originals, Vanves 1979.
Das Brandmal — Emmy Hennings, Das Brandmal. Ein Tagebuch, Berlin 1920; annotated copy in the Schmitt papers, RW 265 no. 22103. Emmy Hennings was the wife of Hugo Ball.

temerataque jura relinquo — “Here I leave peace behind, and violated law.” Pharsalia, I, 225. The words are spoken by Caesar after crossing the Rubicon. Schmitt quoted the line repeatedly; see Dirk Blasius, Carl Schmitt. Preußischer Staatsrat in Hitlers Reich, Göttingen 2001, pp. 69–70; Gespräch, pp. 171–72; BW EJ, p. 446. As late as the end of 1983, he used it as a dedication to Christian Meier; see Zeitschrift für Ideengeschichte, IV/3, 2010, p. 104.
“Carry your incomprehended heart to the dead” — Friedrich Schiller, Demetrius, Act 1:
Go down in silence, and carry to the dead your undiscovered, incomprehended heart.

“Do not let yourself be invited and then disinvited again” — Hans Schomerus, director of the Evangelical Academy in Herrenalb, had invited Schmitt to a conference on “Conservatives and Reactionaries” scheduled for 7–10 May 1953 and asked him to give a lecture on “The Antichrist and Creation.” The invitation went back to a discussion Schmitt had had with Wilhelm Stapel in 1942 about the katechon.
Schomerus also asked him to speak at a conference on the island of Mainau from 16–18 May on the theme “A New Approach to Shakespeare.”
Schmitt immediately accepted, but wanted the title of the first lecture changed to “The Antichrist and What Holds Him Back,” and the title of the second to “Hamlet, God’s Player.”
After protests from Adolf Arndt, Gustav Heinemann, Walter Strauss, and others, Regional Bishop Julius Bender ordered that Schmitt be disinvited.
On 5 May, Schmitt received a telegram from Schomerus:
See Schomerus’s letters to Schmitt, RW 265 nos. 14493–14498; Schmitt’s letters to Schomerus, RW 265 nos. 13505–13506; BW Forsthoff, pp. 396–97.
tutela praesens — “present protection.” Refers to Horace, Carmina IV, 14.43. In: idem, Sämtliche Werke. Lateinisch und deutsch, 10th ed., Munich and Zurich 1985, p. 206.
For Schmitt, tutela praesens was an essential part of political representation:
“Representation is nothing if it is not tutela praesens.”
Dieu existe avant la société des hommes intelligents, et la création n’a fait que le produire à l’univers. Donc Dieu existe avant l’homme; donc Dieu est cause, et l’homme est effet.
“God exists before the society of intelligent human beings, and creation merely brought him forth into the universe. Therefore God exists before man; therefore God is the cause, and man the effect.”
L. G. A. de Bonald, Oeuvres complètes, published by Migne, vol. 1, Paris 1859, col. 481.
tacito rumore Mosella sc. nondum canalisata — “the Moselle flowing with a quiet murmur — namely, the Moselle before it had been canalized.”
With tacito rumore Mosella, Schmitt, whose ancestors came from the Moselle region, quotes the poem Mosella by the late Roman poet Decimus Magnus Ausonius. See ECS, p. 10.
When plans to canalize the Moselle were being considered in the 1950s, Schmitt added the qualification. For example, in a letter to E. Jünger dated 30 December 1955, he wrote:
“In the ‘Conversation with Spranger’ in Ex Captivitate Salus it should read: tacito rumore Mosella sc. nondum canalisata. I am therefore your uncanalizable Moselle man.”
